title: The Magus of Movement: Bratislava to Weybridge
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Pozsony (Bratislava), the birth house below the castle
stops.campa: Rudolf Laban is born on 15 December in Pozsony, the old coronation city on the Danube, son of a rising officer of the Imperial and Royal Army and grandson of soldiers. The house stands under the castle hill, between the river and the vineyards. The city speaks three languages in one breath: Hungarian, German, Slovak. And the boy will keep all his life this habit of the border: no single tongue, no single nation, only the current that moves beneath them all.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935, trans. Lisa Ullmann 1975)
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: The castle hill and the vineyards of the Little Carpathians
stops.campa: The child roams the castle hill and the vine terraces above the town, and there the first theatre happens without a stage: he stages plays for other children among the rocks, conjuring a mountain sprite who guards the crystal heart of the hill. In A Life for Dance he will place the seed here: the conviction, arrived at before words, that the hills, the river, the marching soldiers and the wheeling swifts are all one single moving thing, and that a person could learn its grammar.
suggested_refs: A Life for Dance, chapter on childhood
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Stadttheater Pressburg, the first theatre
stops.campa: In the new Stadttheater, gaslit and gilded, the boy is taken to see opera and pantomime, and he is lost at once. It is not the story that takes him but the moment the curtain rises on bodies arranged in light: an architecture that breathes. He begins building toy theatres at home, cutting figures, moving them through invented processions. His military family smiles at the hobby, not yet knowing it is a vocation announcing itself in the only costume available to a child.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
John Hodgson, Mastering Movement: The Life and Work of Rudolf Laban (2001)

stops.name: Sarajevo, the governor's garrison
stops.campa: The father, now a general and military governor in occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, brings the boy south on garrison journeys. Sarajevo opens before him: minarets and mountains, bazaar and barracks, the call to prayer threading through the bugle calls of the Empire. An officer's son is expected to see fortifications; this one sees processions, ritual gestures, the carriage of porters and horsemen: a whole city as a slow choir of movement. The Orient enters him here and never leaves.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Hadži Sinan tekke, Sarajevo: the dervishes turning
stops.campa: A mullah, friend of the family, leads the boy into the tekke, and there he witnesses the turning of the dervishes: men spinning past exhaustion into radiance, the body used as a door. The canon is exact on what happens next: the boy understands that dance is not decoration but a means of ecstasy and prayer, a technology of the soul. This is the seed of everything: Monte Verità, the movement choirs, the whole cathedral of his later work is founded in this smoky room in Sarajevo.
suggested_refs: A Life for Dance, dervish episode
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Mostar, the old bridge and the sword dances
stops.campa: At Mostar the white bridge leaps the Neretva in a single held breath, and young men dive from its crown into the green water: a dance with death for an audience of the town. In the villages around, Laban watches ritual sword dances and circle dances, kolo upon kolo, and notes that ordinary people, farmers and soldiers, carry dances the way they carry knives: as inheritance. Folk movement, he learns, is older than art and stronger than armies.
suggested_refs: Herzegovinian kolo and sword dance traditions
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Ivan Pass, the mountains seen as movement
stops.campa: Riding with his father's column over the pass between Bosnia and Herzegovina, the boy has the vision the tradition preserves: the mountains themselves are moving, folded, thrust, frozen mid-gesture, and the clouds, the column of soldiers, the eagles above are phrases of one immense composition. Landscape is slow dance; dance is fast landscape. Decades later, in Choreutics, he will build a geometry for this vision. Here it is simply given to him, whole, on a military road.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Wiener Neustadt, the Theresian Military Academy
stops.campa: The family's road is laid out: the eldest son enters the officers' academy at Wiener Neustadt, the oldest military academy in the world. He drills, fences, rides, and finds even here his own subject, for drill is choreography with the joy removed. He watches formations wheel on the parade ground and sees movement choirs in uniform, commanded instead of shared. Within a year he knows he cannot serve two masters. The sword or the dance: the choice is forming.

stops.name: Vienna, the refusal
stops.campa: In 1900 the cadet lays down the commission. He tells his father, the general, the governor, that he will be an artist, and the tradition records the household's grief as a kind of funeral. It is the founding sacrifice of the myth: the son of the army deserts to the body's other discipline. He marries the young painter Martha Fricke, and together they turn west, toward the one city where a body can study itself: Paris.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Paris, arrival at the Gare de l'Est
stops.campa: Laban arrives in Paris in the year of the Exposition Universelle, the city electric with pavilions, moving sidewalks and the new century. He is twenty, disinherited of a military future, married to a painter, owning little but conviction. Paris receives him as it receives all such arrivals: indifferently, which is to say freely. He takes rooms, takes work as an illustrator, and begins the double apprenticeship the canon assigns him: architecture by day, the cabarets' living anatomy by night.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: École des Beaux-Arts, architecture: the body as building
stops.campa: At the École des Beaux-Arts he studies architecture and stage design, and the tradition insists this is no detour: it is here the magus learns that space has laws. Plans, sections, the platonic solids, the proportions of the human figure inscribed in circle and square: he absorbs the architect's faith that form can be notated, transmitted, built again from drawings. One substitution and his life's work appears: let the building move. The dancer is living architecture; the score is its blueprint.
suggested_refs: École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts, Paris

stops.name: Montmartre, the cabarets: the anatomy of the crowd
stops.campa: By night he earns bread drawing caricatures and posters for the revues of Montmartre, and takes the cabaret as his second academy. He watches chanteuses, apaches, can-can lines and drunks with the same clinical tenderness: every body confesses its inner life in its effort, the miser's cramped gesture, the braggart's flung one. Years later his factory studies in England will use exactly this eye. Montmartre teaches him that there are no unexpressive bodies, only unread ones.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Notre-Dame, the cathedral as frozen procession
stops.campa: Standing in the nave of Notre-Dame, the architecture student has the second great vision of the canon: the cathedral is a procession arrested in stone, verticals striving, vaults clasping, the rose window a round dance of light held at its stillest instant. He conceives the converse of his mountain vision: as landscape is slow dance, so sacred building is dance made permanent. A temple, then, could be built of moving bodies alone. The swinging temple, der schwingende Tempel, is conceived here, twenty years before Hamburg dances it.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Montparnasse, the death of Martha
stops.campa: In 1907 Martha Fricke dies, leaving Laban with two small children and a silence the autobiography walks around rather than through. The Paris apprenticeship ends in grief. He is twenty-seven, a widower, an artist without an art yet: painter, illustrator, architect of nothing built. The canon reads the wound plainly: from now on his companions will be schools, troupes, choirs, families of movement assembled and reassembled around him, and no loss will ever again find him standing still.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Vienna, the years of illustration and mourning
stops.campa: He returns east to Vienna and the Habsburg lands, keeping himself and the children by drawing for journals, organizing artists' festivals, moving through the Secession's afterglow. These are the hidden years of the tradition, the chrysalis: outwardly a facile illustrator, inwardly assembling his doctrine of festival, the conviction that modern people are starving for communal celebration, and that the artist's true office is not to perform for them but to set them dancing. In 1910 he marries the singer Maja Lederer and turns to Munich.
sources: Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Munich, Schwabing: the atelier
stops.campa: Laban settles in Schwabing, the bohemian quarter where Kandinsky is dissolving the object and Stefan George is dictating to disciples. Here at thirty he opens an atelier for movement experiment, and the caricaturist becomes a teacher of bodies. He works with breath, with swing, with the scales of gesture, seeking dance freed from ballet's syllabus and from music's tyranny: dance as an autonomous art with its own laws. Schwabing names him at once: not dancer, not master, but magus.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Munich, master of the carnival
stops.campa: At Fasching the artists' quarter goes ritually mad, and Laban is made master of its festivals. He designs and directs the great carnival nights: hundreds of costumed citizens moved through processions, entrances, whirls. He discovers his instrument is not the soloist but the crowd. A banker in a devil's mask dances better than a bored ballerina: the finding is doctrinal. The movement choir is invented here in embryo, at three in the morning, in confetti, before it ever has a name.
suggested_refs: Munich Fasching artists' festivals, photographs c. 1911
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Munich, Suzanne Perrottet and the break from music
stops.campa: Suzanne Perrottet, star pupil of Jaques-Dalcroze at Hellerau, comes to Laban and defects from eurhythmics to his camp: from movement obeying music to movement sovereign. Around them gathers the first circle: musicians, painters, seekers. And Laban formulates the heresy that founds the new German dance: rhythm lives in the body before it lives in sound. He begins teaching dance in silence, to breath and pulse alone. The Dalcroze school takes note of the apostasy; more defectors will follow.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Munich, the school for dance, sound and word
stops.campa: Laban founds his Munich school for Tanz-Ton-Wort: dance, sound and word, a curriculum for the whole expressive human. Pupils improvise with gongs and drums they play themselves; they speak, chant, leap. It is less a conservatory than a rite in daily installments. And already he is planning a bolder vessel: a summer colony where the school can live day and night, on the vegetarian mountain above Lake Maggiore of which all Schwabing whispers, the Mountain of Truth.
sources: Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Monte Verità, Ascona: arrival on the sacred hill
stops.campa: In the summer of 1913 Laban climbs Monte Verità above Ascona and opens his School for Art on the hill of the life-reformers: vegetarians, theosophists, anarchists, sun-worshippers, the prophet Gusto Gräser in his rock grotto below. The colony gives him what no city can: bodies freed of corsets and shoes, air, meadow, lake, and a community already living as if the new age had come. The hill and the magus recognize each other. Here the new dance will be born outdoors, in daylight.
suggested_refs: Johann Adam Meisenbach photographs of the Laban school, Monte Verità

stops.name: Monte Verità: Mary Wigman climbs the hill
stops.campa: Mary Wigman arrives from Hellerau on the painter Emil Nolde's advice, a fierce, unfinished dancer whom Dalcroze's method could not hold. Laban sees her improvise and knows what has come to him: not a pupil but a force to be unbound. She becomes his assistant, his sparring partner, the first flame of Ausdruckstanz. The canon marks this meeting as the hinge of German dance: the master with the doctrine and the dancer with the daimon, met on a meadow above the lake.
suggested_refs: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: The meadow, sun-worship and the first movement choirs
stops.campa: At dawn the school greets the sun with swinging scales of movement; by day it works barefoot in the meadow; at dusk it dances rounds that close the day like a liturgy. Laban leads with drum and lyre, bearded, half prophet and half engineer, testing the choir forms he will later give to whole cities. The famous photographs are made here: white-clad and unclad bodies wheeling on the grass, the lake below, the new century briefly innocent. The movement choir is born as sun-worship.

stops.name: Monte Verità, the dance farm: the little kingdom
stops.campa: The second summer establishes the colony as a working dance farm, his little kingdom, as he calls it, where pupils garden, cook, weave costumes and dance, art and life composted together. Wigman, Perrottet and the circle deepen the experiments: swings, scales, the beginnings of a spatial harmony modeled on crystal forms. Laban dreams the school as the germ of a coming festival culture for all of Europe. Europe, that same June, is dreaming otherwise: at Sarajevo, his boyhood city, a pistol is being loaded.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Ascona, August 1914: the war breaks over the hill
stops.campa: War is declared while the summer school is in session. The omen the canon preserves: the assassination that fired the world was done in Sarajevo, where the child Laban first saw the dervishes turn. The seed-place and the wound-place are one. Pupils scatter to their mobilizing nations within days. Laban, Hungarian subject on neutral soil, stays as the meadow empties, understanding that the festival culture he prophesied has been answered by its exact inversion: the mass choreography of armies.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Zurich, the wartime school
stops.campa: Laban moves the work to Zurich, neutral hive of exiles, spies and prophets, and opens his school of dance, sound and word. Mary Wigman is his assistant; by day the studio drills swings and scales, by night Laban sits over graph paper hunting the alphabet of movement. Around them the city fills with every avant-garde that war has washed out of Europe. The school is poor, cold and incandescent: the laboratory where Ausdruckstanz is refined from rite into discipline.
sources: Mary Wigman, The Language of Dance (1966)
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Cabaret Voltaire, Spiegelgasse 1: the Dada adjacency
stops.campa: Five doors from Lenin's lodging, Hugo Ball opens the Cabaret Voltaire, and Laban's dancers are drawn into its orbit: Sophie Taeuber, Käthe Wulff, Suzanne Perrottet dance to Dada's drums in masks by Janco. Laban himself keeps a magus's distance, attending, lending dancers, withholding allegiance: Dada dismembers the arts, he is assembling one. But the canon counts the adjacency as formative on both sides: abstract dance enters Dada from his studio, and Dada's permission to begin from zero enters him.
sources: Hugo Ball, Flight Out of Time (1927)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Galerie Dada, Bahnhofstrasse: abstract dances
stops.campa: At the Galerie Dada the collaboration peaks: to Hugo Ball's sound-poems, Sophie Taeuber dances abstractions in a shaman's mask while Laban's pupils perform choric works for an audience of the exiled avant-garde. Ball writes in his diary of dancers as marionettes of a new mythology. The tradition fixes this as the crossing-point of the century's two escapes from the old world: the word dissolved into sound, the body dissolved into pure motion, and Laban's grammar underlies the second.
suggested_refs: Hugo Ball diary, Flight Out of Time
sources: Hugo Ball, Flight Out of Time (1927)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Zurich, the lodge and the grammar of movement
stops.campa: The war years are Laban's hermetic period. He is received into the esoteric currents pooling in Zurich: the Ordo Templi Orientis of Theodor Reuss charters a lodge with Laban among its lights, and he reads the body through crystal, planet and rite. At night he fills notebooks with signs: the first true drafts of a script for movement, tried and discarded and tried again. The canon does not blush at the occult apprenticeship; the notation that conquered the world was incubated in a lodge.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Monte Verità: Sang an die Sonne, the sun festival
stops.campa: At the close of the great pacifist and esoteric congress on Monte Verità, Laban stages Sang an die Sonne across a whole night of the mountain: the sun's descent danced at evening; at midnight, before Gusto Gräser's grotto, the demons of the night; at dawn the choir greets the rising sun as the promise that the war-winter of the world will end. Wigman and the school dance it on the meadow with torches. It is the movement choir consecrated: liturgy for a religion of the body, performed while the guns hold Europe.

stops.name: Zurich, the illness
stops.campa: As the war ends the influenza takes him, and on its heels a general collapse of body and fortunes. The school scatters; Wigman leaves the master's shadow to become a fate of her own. Laban, who preached the body as temple, lies fevered in a poor room while armistice bells ring over the lake. The canon reads the illness as initiatory: the magus is broken down to be rebuilt for the German decade, and from his sickbed he keeps drawing signs for a script no one yet believes in.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Nuremberg, convalescence in the north
stops.campa: Penniless and still weak, Laban crosses into defeated Germany and convalesces at Nuremberg, the old imperial city of clockmakers and Meistersinger. Inflation eats what little he has; the country around him is hungry, humiliated and strangely ready: a nation whose gestures have been shattered and must be relearned. He recognizes his congregation. Germany after the war will receive the new dance as a starving man receives bread, and the sick Hungarian in the Nuremberg attic is carrying the recipe.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Stuttgart, Die Welt des Tänzers
stops.campa: In Stuttgart Laban publishes his first book, Die Welt des Tänzers, The Dancer's World, part treatise, part scripture: the dancer as a complete mode of being, thinking in movement as others think in words. The book makes him overnight the theorist-prophet of the new German dance. Around the Stuttgart studio a school and company begin to crystallize, and a letter of this year states the mission in his own hand.
stops.quote: first to give Dance and the Dancer their proper value as Art and the Artist, and second to enforce the influence of dance education on the warped psyche of our time
stops.quote_source: Laban, letter to a friend, 1920 (cited in Cabinet magazine, issue 36)
suggested_refs: Die Welt des Tänzers, first edition (Stuttgart: Walter Seifert, 1920)
sources: Rudolf Laban, Die Welt des Tänzers (1920)

stops.name: Stuttgart: Kurt Jooss comes to the master
stops.campa: A stocky young music student named Kurt Jooss finds his way to the Stuttgart studio and is remade within a month: he abandons everything else for the new dance. Laban takes him as pupil, then as right hand. The canon savors the symmetry it is planting: eighteen years hence, when the master flees the Reich in ruins, it is this pupil's door in Devon that will open to him. The Tanzbühne Laban, the master's touring temple of dancers, assembles around them.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Mannheim, Nationaltheater: the Tannhäuser Bacchanal
stops.campa: Engaged at the Mannheim National Theatre, Laban choreographs the Bacchanal of Tannhäuser: the Venusberg orgy danced not as ballet divertissement but as Ausdruckstanz, weight and swing and ecstasy in Wagner's own house of the bourgeoisie. It is the new dance's first conquest of the opera stage, and a prophecy: nine years later Bayreuth itself will summon him for the same scene. The scandalized and the converted leave by the same doors, arguing.
suggested_refs: Nationaltheater Mannheim, old house on Schillerplatz

stops.name: Hamburg, Der schwingende Tempel
stops.campa: In Hamburg, home port of the Tanzbühne Laban, he stages Der schwingende Tempel, The Swinging Temple, the vision from Notre-Dame made flesh at last: a temple built of nothing but moving bodies, chorus upon chorus swinging through crystal pathways, architecture that breathes and is gone. The company dances it without star roles; the building is the protagonist. The tradition ranks it as the master's manifesto-work, the proof that his choirs can raise invisible cathedrals.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)
Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Hamburg Stadtpark, the movement choirs of workers
stops.campa: Laban founds the first Bewegungschöre, movement choirs, for the people of Hamburg: clerks, dockers, shopgirls, war widows, gathered by the hundred in halls and in the Stadtpark to dance great communal forms under his pupils' direction. No audience, no stars; the dance is done for the doing, as choirs sing. The idea spreads through Germany like fire through August grass: dozens of cities raise Laban choirs within the decade. The carnival master of Schwabing has become the liturgist of an amateur nation.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Zagreb, the stranded troupe
stops.campa: The Tanzbühne tours the Balkans and is wrecked there: in Zagreb the money fails, the impresario vanishes, and the company is stranded hungry in the lands of Laban's boyhood journeys. A Life for Dance tells it as picaresque, dancers pawning costumes, the master conjuring passage home city by city, but the canon hears the deeper note: the South that gave him the dervish-seed now takes his theatre from him, turning him from touring works toward the imperishable work, the script. What cannot be stranded is notation.
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Würzburg, the Choreographisches Institut founded
stops.campa: At Würzburg Laban founds the Choreographisches Institut, the first research institute in history to take dance as a science: notation, choreology, the harmony of space studied as astronomers study orbits. Pupils trace the icosahedron's diagonals with their limbs; scribes test sign after sign. The magus now has his observatory. Around it his empire is at high tide: Laban schools in every major German city, choirs in dozens more, his name a movement in both senses of the word.
sources: Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Magdeburg, the First German Dancers' Congress
stops.campa: At the great theatre exhibition in Magdeburg the German dancers convene for the first time as an estate of the realm, and Laban stands at the center of the parliament he has effectively summoned. Ausdruckstanz debates itself: stage dance against choir dance, Wigman's daimon against Laban's harmonies. The congress ends with the new dance acknowledged as a national art. What the church council is to a young faith, Magdeburg is to German dance, and Laban is its presiding, disputed patriarch.
sources: Susan Manning, Ecstasy and the Demon (1993)
Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Berlin: the Institute moves to the capital
stops.campa: The Choreographisches Institut moves to Berlin, into the roaring capital of the Republic: Weimar Berlin, where every art is being rebuilt from first principles and the body is the decade's obsession. Laban is now a public figure: feuilletons, lectures, disciples, rivals. In the Institute's studios the notation reaches its final form, sign by sign, staff by staff. The city that measures everything is given the man who has measured movement itself.
sources: Evelyn Doerr, Rudolf Laban: The Dancer of the Crystal (2008)

stops.name: Essen, the Second Dancers' Congress: movement gets its alphabet
stops.campa: At the Second Dancers' Congress in Essen, Laban rises and presents Kinetographie: the finished script of movement, the work of a quarter century since the Beaux-Arts drawing boards. Direction, level, duration, weight: any human movement, written; any written movement, danced again by strangers unborn. The journal Schrifttanz is founded to carry the script into the world. The congress understands what it is witnessing: dance, mortal for all of human history, has been given an alphabet. Labanotation is loosed upon time.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

segments.name: The State Theatres and the Fall

stops.name: Bayreuth, Festspielhaus: the Bacchanal on the Green Hill
stops.campa: Siegfried Wagner summons Laban to Bayreuth to choreograph the Tannhäuser Bacchanal for the Festival: Toscanini in the pit, the Wagner shrine on its Green Hill, and in the Venusberg the wheeling bodies of Ausdruckstanz where ballet convention had always stood. The dervish-seed comes full circle: the ecstatic turn, seen by a boy in Sarajevo, is danced in the holiest theatre of the German imagination. The production triumphs and is repeated the following summer. The magus stands at the summit of the German stage.

stops.name: Berlin, Staatsoper Unter den Linden: ballet master of the state
stops.campa: Laban is appointed director of movement and dance at the Prussian State Theatres, seated at the Staatsoper Unter den Linden: the barefoot prophet of Monte Verità now master of the state's own dancers. He reforms the ballet toward the new dance, notates repertory, administers, negotiates. The canon notes the ambivalence it will later need: the man who dreamed festival culture for free communities now holds office from the state, and states change hands. Within three years, this one does.
suggested_refs: Laban as ballet director, press photographs c. 1931

stops.name: Berlin, the Deutsche Tanzbühne: the harness of the new masters
stops.campa: The Reich takes the theatres, and Goebbels' ministry sets Laban over the Deutsche Tanzbühne: German dance gathered under one office, his office. The canon does not look away: the master serves, organizes festivals, believes his art can remain his own inside their harness, believes the choirs he built for free citizens can survive being marched. It is the magus's error and the tradition tells it as tragedy, not alibi: he mistakes the Reich for one more patron, and the Reich mistakes him, briefly, for one more instrument.
sources: Marion Kant and Lilian Karina, Hitler's Dancers (2003)
Susan Manning, Ecstasy and the Demon (1993)

stops.name: Berlin, A Life for Dance published
stops.campa: Laban publishes his autobiography, Ein Leben für den Tanz: a magus's memoir in which the dervishes, the mountain visions, the sacred hill and the swinging temple are set down as the stations of a single calling. Written at the height of his official power, it reads now as unknowing farewell to the German world that is about to expel him: within a year of its printing, everything it celebrates will be forbidden ground.
stops.quote: For a dancer to lose his mobility is the same as for a painter to lose his eyesight or a musician to go deaf.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935; trans. Lisa Ullmann, 1975)
suggested_refs: Ein Leben für den Tanz, first edition (Dresden: Carl Reissner, 1935)
sources: Rudolf Laban, A Life for Dance (1935)

stops.name: Dietrich-Eckart-Bühne, the dress rehearsal of Vom Tauwind
stops.campa: For the Olympic festival Laban prepares his greatest choir work: Vom Tauwind und der neuen Freude, Of the Thawing Wind and the New Joy, a thousand amateur dancers from movement choirs across Germany, verses after Nietzsche, spring wind overcoming winter, on the vast new open-air stage in the Grunewald. At the dress rehearsal twenty thousand watch. Goebbels sits among them in the June dark and sees, correctly, that nothing in this surging, free-breathing mass belongs to him. The thaw-wind blows once, before witnesses, and is never permitted again.
suggested_refs: Vom Tauwind rehearsal photographs, Laban Collection
sources: Marion Kant and Lilian Karina, Hitler's Dancers (2003)

stops.name: Berlin, the ban and the fall
stops.campa: Goebbels kills the work after the rehearsal: it is dressed in their clothes, his diary sneers, and has nothing to do with them. The performance is struck from the Olympic program; Laban's offices are stripped from him piece by piece, his salary cut, his notation society dissolved, watchers set on his house. The fall is total and the canon reads it as the myth requires: the moment the magus's art faces the Reich directly, the Reich recognizes an enemy. His health breaks under the surveillance winter.
sources: Marion Kant and Lilian Karina, Hitler's Dancers (2003)

stops.name: Schloss Banz, the winter of internment
stops.campa: Out of office and out of favor, Laban is kept through the winter at Schloss Banz, the old monastery-castle above the Main: a genteel quarantine, watched and shelved. The man who commanded a thousand dancers walks the terraces alone, ill, past sixty visions and a confiscated life's work. The tradition keeps this station as the dark night, the magus in the disused abbey, stripped of school, institute, choirs, theatre and country, with nothing left but what no state can requisition: the script, and the space inside the icosahedron.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Paris, the flight
stops.campa: In August 1937, sick and closely watched, Laban obtains leave to attend a congress in Paris, and does not come back. The city of his apprenticeship receives the fugitive it once received as a bridegroom: he arrives with almost nothing, thirty-seven years after arriving with almost nothing. The Exposition's pavilions glitter on the Seine, Speer's German tower glaring at the Soviet one across the water, the world rehearsing its next war, while between them an old man with a broken heart quietly fails to go home.
suggested_refs: Paris Exposition Internationale 1937, German and Soviet pavilions
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Paris, the destitute winter
stops.campa: The winter in Paris is the myth's lowest station: the founder of European modern dance, stateless in fact if not in law, ill, aged, poor, sheltering where friends can place him. The choirs dance on in Germany under other names; his own name is being scraped from their histories. Word passes along the refugee network to Devon, where Kurt Jooss, the Stuttgart pupil, himself four years an exile for refusing to abandon his Jewish colleagues, hears in what state the master is. A door begins to open across the Channel.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Dover, landfall in England
stops.campa: At the turn of 1938 Laban crosses the Channel and comes ashore at Dover, fifty-eight years old, carrying a lifetime in a few cases: notebooks, scores in his own script, the icosahedron folded flat in his mind. England knows almost nothing of him; the language is not his; the body of work is all in the tongue of the country that cast him out. The canon marks the landfall as the last of his border-crossings; the child of the triple-tongued Danube city takes his final nationality: movement.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Dartington Hall, the refuge
stops.campa: In February 1938 Laban comes to Dartington Hall in Devon, the Elmhirsts' utopian estate where Kurt Jooss and Sigurd Leeder have rebuilt their school in exile. The pupil receives the master: Jooss meets him at the door of the mediaeval hall, and the German dance, scattered by the Reich, is regathered in an English garden. Laban arrives broken: the Dartington memory preserves how frail, how extinguished he seems. And the estate simply lets him be: a room, meals, the park, no demands. The rebuilding begins with rest.
suggested_refs: Photograph of the Jooss family with Laban, c. 1938

stops.name: Dartington gardens, Lisa Ullmann and the recovery
stops.campa: In the gardens above the Dart the magus mends. Lisa Ullmann, a young teacher of the Jooss-Leeder school, takes his recovery in hand: translator, organizer, disciple, and from now to the end his companion and the executor of his mission in England. He walks the terraces, watches English trees move in English wind, and begins again at the beginning, as he always does: observing. The canon pairs them henceforth: Laban the failing oracle, Ullmann the unfailing voice that carries him to a new nation.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Dartington, writing Choreutics
stops.campa: Through 1939, as Europe arms, Laban sits at Dartington writing Choreutics: the summa of the space-harmony he has pursued since the Herzegovinian passes, the scales and rings of movement threaded through the icosahedron, the mountain vision finally given its geometry. War will delay the book a quarter century; it appears only after his death. But the manuscript is the treasure the exile saved, written in an English garden while the world that formed it burns its own libraries.
stops.quote: Movement is, so to speak, living architecture — living in the sense of changing emplacements as well as changing cohesion.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Laban, Choreutics (written 1939, published London: Macdonald & Evans, 1966)

stops.name: London, enemy alien in the invasion summer
stops.campa: France falls, invasion is expected on the Devon coast, and the south-west is closed to enemy aliens: the refugee who fled the Reich is now, by paper, its national. Laban and Ullmann must leave Dartington. They pass through a London filling with sandbags and separations, tribunals weighing the loyalty of exiles. He is old enough and ill enough to escape internment, and poor enough that it hardly matters. The tradition notes the irony without bitterness: England mistrusts him with one hand and shelters him with the other.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Newtown, Wales, the quiet valley
stops.campa: Laban and Ullmann settle in Newtown in the Severn valley of mid-Wales, far from the bombed cities. Ullmann teaches movement to teachers and schoolchildren; Laban gardens, draws, and watches the Welsh hill farmers work: scythe, pitchfork, the economy of laboring bodies. In the observation the last great turn of his thought begins: from the dancer's effort to the worker's effort, from the stage to the loom and the lathe. The valley years look idle and are seminal, as the canon's quiet chapters always are.
sources: Valerie Preston-Dunlop, Rudolf Laban: An Extraordinary Life (1998)

stops.name: Manchester, F. C. Lawrence: industry calls the magus
stops.campa: The industrial consultant F. C. Lawrence, alerted through Dartington's network, seeks Laban out: Britain's factories are full of untrained wartime workers wasting strength, and here is the one man alive who can read effort itself. Laban moves to Manchester, black city of looms and rain, and the strangest partnership of the myth begins: the barefoot prophet of Monte Verità walking factory floors with a management accountant, watching women lift, carry, wrap, and seeing in each act weight, time, space and flow.
sources: Rudolf Laban and F. C. Lawrence, Effort (1947)

stops.name: The factories, the effort studies
stops.campa: In the mills and works, tyre plants in Manchester, the Mars confectionery lines at Slough, Laban studies workers as he once studied dervishes and dancers. He retunes tasks to the body's natural rhythms: the right worker matched to the right effort, strain converted to swing. Output rises; fatigue falls; dance teaches industry to move. The canon delights in the reversal: the art the Reich called degenerate is now war work for Britain. And in the constancy beneath it: he has never studied anything but the moving human, anywhere.
sources: Rudolf Laban and F. C. Lawrence, Effort (1947)

stops.name: Manchester, Oxford Road: the Art of Movement Studio
stops.campa: With the war ended, Lisa Ullmann opens the Art of Movement Studio on Oxford Road, Manchester, with Laban as its presiding spirit. Teachers, dancers and factory trainers come to learn the new subject England will shortly write into its schools: movement itself, weight-time-space-flow, the education of the whole moving child. From this plain northern studio, Laban's third empire spreads: not theatres now, not choirs, but classrooms. The exile who arrived with nothing has seeded a national curriculum.
suggested_refs: Art of Movement Studio, Manchester photographs

stops.name: Manchester, the English books
stops.campa: In quick succession the doctrine is recast in English: Effort with Lawrence in 1947, Modern Educational Dance in 1948, The Mastery of Movement on the Stage in 1950. The German prophet becomes an English author, plain-spoken, practical, addressing teachers and actors where he once addressed initiates. The mystic core survives translation intact: the books open from a single axiom that had been true since Sarajevo.
stops.quote: Man moves in order to satisfy a need.
stops.quote_source: Rudolf Laban, The Mastery of Movement on the Stage (London: Macdonald & Evans, 1950)
suggested_refs: The Mastery of Movement on the Stage (1950)
sources: Rudolf Laban, The Mastery of Movement on the Stage (1950)
Rudolf Laban and F. C. Lawrence, Effort (1947)

stops.name: Addlestone, the Studio at Woburn Hill
stops.campa: In 1953 the Art of Movement Studio moves south to Woburn Hill at Addlestone in Surrey, on land given by the Elmhirsts' son: Dartington's generosity following him to the end. Here the old magus keeps his last court: mornings in the studio watching classes, afternoons among manuscripts, crystal models and effort graphs, evenings drawing. Students remember a white-bearded man of uncanny lightness who could read a person's whole nature from their walk across the lawn. The work turns late toward movement therapy: healing, the first and final use of the dervishes' door.

Late photographs of Laban at Addlestone

stops.name: Weybridge, the death of the magus
stops.campa: Rudolf Laban dies at Weybridge on the first of July 1958, in the green corner of Surrey where his last studio dances on without pause. The canon closes the circle it opened on the Danube: the boy who saw the dervishes turn in Sarajevo has left the turning world a script to remember its dances by, choirs on three continents, a geometry of the soul's directions, and schools that need no master present; for movement, he taught, is the one estate that cannot be confiscated. The body stops; the notation does not.
